kurals.tamil:
பெறுமவற்றுள் யாமறிவது இல்லை அறிவறிந்த
மக்கட்பேறு அல்ல பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Perumavatrul Yaamarivadhu Illai Arivarindha,
Makkatperu Alla Pira.
kurals.meaning: Among all the good things a person may come to possess, we know of none greater than having children who have learned what is worth knowing.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone gives you a huge pile of presents — toys, money, a big house. This kural says that if you also had a child who grows up kind and clever, that child would be the best present of all, better than everything else in the pile put together.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter on progeny by ranking it above every other பேறு (pēṟu, "gain, acquisition") a householder can obtain, and the qualifier is decisive: not merely மக்கட்பேறு (makkaṭ-pēṟu, the getting of children) but அறிவறிந்த மக்கட்பேறு — children who have "known what is to be known." The reduplicative phrase அறிவு அறிந்த is characteristically Kural-like compression: it makes discernment, not mere biological succession, the thing being praised. Parimēlaḻakar, the fourteenth-century commentator, frames the whole adhikāram through the pan-Indic doctrine of the three debts (ṛṇa-traya) owed by the twice-born — to the sages, discharged by study; to the gods, by sacrifice; and to the ancestors (தென்புலத்தார், ten-pulattār), discharged only by begetting offspring — which is why the chapter follows immediately on marriage and the worth of a wife. Notably, Valluvar himself never invokes that ritual apparatus: he argues purely from the sweetness and social worth of the thing itself, which is part of why the text reads as equally at home in Jain, Śaiva and secular frameworks. The use of the first-person plural யாம் ("we know of none") is also worth marking — it is the voice of considered human judgement rather than revelation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Vedic doctrine of the three debts (ṛṇa-traya) holds that every person is born owing three debts — to the sages, discharged by study of scripture; to the gods, discharged by sacrifice; and to the ancestors, which can be discharged in one way only, by begetting offspring to continue the line.
hinduism.explanation: In this framework a childless life leaves a structural obligation permanently unpaid, so progeny is not one good among many but a settling of accounts with the whole chain of generations behind you.
hinduism.tie_back: Both traditions place children at the very top of the ledger of what a householder can acquire — and Valluvar's own classical commentator Parimelalagar reads this exact kural through this doctrine.
hinduism.source: Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10.5 (the doctrine of the three debts, ṛṇa-traya)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Described as a doctrine rather than quoted, because English renderings of the Taittirīya passage vary widely; the conceptual match is strong and is the one Valluvar's own commentator applies here.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist interrupts a poem about the futility of human striving — building houses, guarding cities, rising early to eat the bread of sorrows — to say that children are not something you earn but something given, and that they are the real return on a life.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the psalm sets children above every other acquisition a person labours for.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against the KJV; both texts explicitly rank children as the supreme thing one receives.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one's] hope.”
islam.explanation: The verse concedes that children are genuinely among life's beauties, but ranks them below the lasting righteous deeds that outlive this world.
islam.tie_back: Both texts put children at the summit of worldly goods, though the Qur'an then relativises even that summit in a way Valluvar's couplet does not.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, but the Qur'an subordinates children to enduring deeds whereas the Kural makes them the highest gain outright — a real difference in ranking.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Abram said, Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?”
judaism.explanation: God has just promised Abram an exceedingly great reward, and Abram's reply is essentially that no reward counts for anything while he has no child of his own.
judaism.tie_back: Abram states the Kural's thesis negatively: every other gain is worthless set beside the gain of a child.
judaism._accuracy_note: Standard KJV wording; a strong narrative match, though Abram's concern is dynastic inheritance rather than Valluvar's emphasis on the child's discernment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Considering these five reasons / The Wise wish for a child, thinking: / Supported he will support us, / He will do his duties for us, / He will maintain his heritage, / And practice according to wealth, / Also he will make offerings / To relatives who pass away.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha here lays out, without disapproval, exactly why householders rationally want children — mutual support, continuity of the family line, and the merit-offerings made for the dead.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, this is an unembarrassed householder's-eye accounting of why a child is the most valuable thing a family can obtain.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.39, Puttasutta, vv. 506–507 (trans. Ānandajoti Bhikkhu, Buddhist Wisdom Verses)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Ānandajoti Bhikkhu's verse translation; a close functional parallel, though framed as five practical reasons rather than a single superlative claim.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Aegeus, king of Athens, having no child by either of his two wives, travelled to Delphi to ask the oracle how he might obtain a son; the god gave him a riddling answer about not loosening the wineskin's mouth until he reached home, and his pursuit of an heir eventually produced Theseus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story presumes a king who has everything a king can have, and for whom the single unobtained good — a son — is worth a journey to the god himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Aegeus enacts the Kural's ranking: throne, city and wealth already in hand, yet the one gain still worth seeking is a child.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the myth; the match is on the desperate valuation of offspring, but the Greek story is about dynastic succession and says nothing about the child's wisdom.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that parents are fond of their children as of something of themselves, while children are fond of parents as of something they came out of — and that parents know their offspring to be theirs more surely than offspring know their parentage.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the parent–child bond is the most natural of all friendships precisely because a child is, in a real sense, an extension of the parent's own being.
philosophy.tie_back: This grounds philosophically why the Kural can call children the supreme acquisition: what one acquires in a child is a second self.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased rather than quoted because translations of this passage differ considerably; the argument is accurately represented but Aristotle is explaining the bond, not ranking goods.

kurals.tamil:
எழுபிறப்பும் தீயவை தீண்டா பழிபிறங்காப்
பண்புடை மக்கட் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ezhupirappum Theeyavai Theendaa Pazhipirangaap,
Panbudai Makkat Perin.
kurals.meaning: If one begets children of good character, against whom no reproach can be raised, then through all seven births no evil will come near.
kurals.elementary: Think of a family like a long relay race, with each generation passing the baton on. This kural says that if you raise children who do good and never give anyone a reason to blame them, the whole race stays clean — trouble never catches up with your family, not for a very, very long time.
kurals.university: The phrase எழுபிறப்பு (ezhu-piṟappu, "seven births") invokes the classical Indian reckoning of the sevenfold cycle of embodied existence, and Parimēlaḻakar's gloss here is explicitly transmigrational: the parent's accumulated evil karma is worn away by the meritorious acts a virtuous child performs on their behalf. The key qualifier is பழிபிறங்காப் பண்புடை — character (paṇpu) so ordered that பழி (paḻi, public blame or reproach) never rises around it. Valluvar thus binds an other-worldly promise to an entirely this-worldly test: the proof of the child's virtue is that no one can speak ill of them. Whether "seven births" is read literally as rebirths (the Jain and Hindu reading) or idiomatically as "seven generations" — which is how the modern commentator M. Karunanidhi renders it — the structural claim is the same: a child's good conduct is retroactively protective of those who produced them. That inversion of the usual direction of moral influence, from child upward to parent, is what makes the couplet distinctive.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Because a son delivers (trāyate) his father from the hell called Put, he was therefore called put-tra (a deliverer from Put) by the Self-existent (Svayambhū) himself.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu offers a folk etymology in which the very Sanskrit word for son, putra, encodes the son's function: to pull his father out of a particular hell after death.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the same claim as the Kural — that a child's existence and virtue shield the parent from evil across the cycle of births.
hinduism.source: Manusmṛti 9.138 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East, 1886)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Bühler's standard translation; a near one-to-one match on the mechanism of post-mortem deliverance through offspring.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb promises that a righteous person's integrity spills forward onto the generation that follows them.
christianity.tie_back: It shares the Kural's intuition that moral standing flows along a family line, but it runs in the opposite direction — parent blessing child, rather than child protecting parent.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim but a weak match: the direction of moral transfer is reversed, and Christianity has no doctrine of seven births for the Kural's central image to land on.

islam.quote_or_event: “When a man dies, his acts come to an end, but three, recurring charity, or knowledge (by which people) benefit, or a pious child, who prays for him (for the deceased).”
islam.explanation: The hadith names three things that keep generating reward for a person after death, and one of them is a righteous child whose prayers continue to reach the parent.
islam.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's mechanism: the parent's post-mortem condition is improved by the child's goodness.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 1631, Book of Wills (narrated by Abū Hurayrah)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Sunnah.com; the only gap is that Islam has one afterlife rather than seven births.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud states the principle that a son can confer merit on his father, but a father cannot confer merit on his son — illustrated by the wicked king Amon, who is held to have retained a share in the World to Come on account of his righteous son Josiah.
judaism.explanation: Merit in this rabbinic discussion flows upward only: a child's righteousness can rescue a parent's standing, but not the reverse.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact claim — that a blameless child's character reaches backward to shield the one who bore them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Rendered as a paraphrase of the principle because English translations of the Aramaic 'berā mezakkeh abbā' vary; the conceptual match, including the one-way direction of merit, is unusually precise.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He will maintain his heritage, / And practice according to wealth, / Also he will make offerings / To relatives who pass away.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the reasons the Buddha says wise householders want children is that a child will make merit-offerings on behalf of dead relatives — a transfer of benefit to those who can no longer act for themselves.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the child an active agent of relief for the parent beyond this life.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.39, Puttasutta, v. 507 (trans. Ānandajoti Bhikkhu, Buddhist Wisdom Verses)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the mechanism matches (offerings benefiting the departed) but Buddhism frames it as merit dedication, not as evil being prevented from touching the parent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the oxen were not ready, the brothers Cleobis and Biton yoked themselves to the cart and drew their mother, priestess of Hera, all the way to the temple; the watching Argives praised her for such sons, and she prayed the goddess grant them the best thing a human can receive — whereupon they fell asleep in the temple and never woke.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus tells the story as Solon's example of true human happiness: sons whose conduct honours their mother so visibly that the community credits her for them, and the goddess seals it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, blameless children are what keeps evil from reaching the parent — here the mother's happiness is made secure precisely by her sons' virtue.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the episode; the good-children-protect-the-parent theme is present, but there is no rebirth framework and the sons' reward is death, which cuts against the Kural's tone.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato argues in the Laws that the human race is by its nature a partner of all time, and that a person attains to immortality not by outliving death but by leaving children, and children's children, so that the line never breaks.
philosophy.explanation: Marriage law in Plato's ideal city is grounded on this: procreation is how a mortal being participates in something that does not end.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts make offspring the mechanism by which a person's fate extends safely across spans of time they will not personally live through.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Accurate paraphrase of Plato's argument, but he speaks of continuity and immortality of the line rather than of evil being warded off across seven births.

kurals.tamil:
தம்பொருள் என்பதம் மக்கள் அவர்பொருள்
தம்தம் வினையான் வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thamporul Enpadham Makkal Avarporul,
Thamdham Vinaiyaan Varum.
kurals.meaning: The wise say that one's children are one's true wealth; and whatever wealth those children come to have arrives through the deeds each of them performs.
kurals.elementary: Grown-ups sometimes call money their "treasure." This kural says the real treasure is your children. And here's the second part: nobody can just hand a child a good life the way you hand over a coin — what each child ends up with comes from the things they themselves do.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a deliberate double use of பொருள் (poruḷ, "wealth, substance, thing of worth"): children are the parents' poruḷ, and the children in turn have a poruḷ of their own, which arrives by வினை (viṉai, "deed, act, karma"). Parimēlaḻakar reads the second line as meaning that the good deeds children perform on their parents' behalf return to the parents as wealth; Maṇakkuṭavar and several moderns read it more directly, that each person's fortune follows from their own acts. Valluvar's compression permits both, and the ambiguity is productive: the family is a genuine economy of worth, yet no share in it is transferable by mere inheritance. The phrase தம்தம் ("each one's own") is the load-bearing word — it individuates moral responsibility inside a verse that has just made the family a single unit of value. That tension between collective wealth and non-transferable desert is what makes this the philosophically sharpest couplet in the chapter, and it anticipates the Kural's later chapter on ஊழ் (Fate).

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Upaniṣad teaches that a person is made of desire — as their desire is, so is their resolve; as their resolve, so the deed they do; and as the deed they do, so is what they come to inherit.
hinduism.explanation: This is one of the earliest formulations of karma as personal moral causation: what accrues to a person follows from what that person has actually done, not from station or lineage.
hinduism.tie_back: It is precisely the Kural's second line — each one's wealth comes by each one's own deeds.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased rather than quoted because English renderings of this dense passage differ sharply; the doctrinal match with the couplet's second line is very close.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb makes the generations each other's ornament: the old are crowned by their descendants, and the young are honoured by their parentage.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the Kural's first line — offspring counted as the substance and glory of a family — but not its second, which insists each person's fortune is self-earned.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; covers the 'children are wealth' half well, but says the opposite of the Kural on inherited versus earned standing.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives, And that his effort is going to be seen.”
islam.explanation: The verses deny that anyone can be credited or debited with another's account: what a person has is what a person has worked for.
islam.tie_back: This is a direct scriptural statement of the Kural's claim that each child's wealth comes by that child's own deeds.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on the second line, though the Qur'anic verses are not about children specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.”
judaism.explanation: Ezekiel is correcting a popular proverb about children's teeth being set on edge by their parents' sour grapes, and insisting that moral accounts are strictly individual.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's second line stated as law: what belongs to each comes from each one's own doing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a precise match to the second half of the couplet, and notably in tension with Kural 62's transferable merit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Student, beings are owners of kammas, heirs of kammas, they have kammas as their progenitor, kammas as their kin, kammas as their homing-place. It is kammas that differentiate beings according to inferiority and superiority.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha answers a young brahmin who wants to know why people are born into such unequal circumstances: the inheritance that actually matters is not property or birth but one's own accumulated action.
buddhism.tie_back: The Pali even uses the vocabulary of inheritance to say what the Kural says — the real estate anyone comes into is their own deeds.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikāya 135, Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta (trans. Ñāṇamoli Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Ñāṇamoli's translation; an unusually exact conceptual and lexical match to the couplet's second line.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Thou too, my friend, for I see that thou art comely and tall, be thou valiant, that many an one of men yet to be born may praise thee.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena, disguised as Mentes, tells Telemachus that his father's estate is being eaten away and that he cannot go on relying on Odysseus' name — he must act, and earn a reputation of his own.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The goddess makes the Kural's point to a son's face: the wealth and honour that will be yours must come from your own deeds.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 1.301–302 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1919)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against the Murray Loeb text; strong on self-earned standing, but the episode is about heroic reputation rather than a family's wealth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus instructs the student never to say of anything that it has been lost, but that it has been given back — and to apply this to a child as much as to an estate, since both were only ever on loan.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, calling a child "mine" in the possessive sense is a category error that guarantees suffering; what one has is custody, not ownership.
philosophy.tie_back: It qualifies the Kural's opening claim in exactly the way the couplet's own second line does: children may be called one's wealth, but they are not one's property.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased rather than quoted since Carter's and Higginson's renderings differ; the corrective it offers to 'children are my wealth' is genuine but is Epictetus's own emphasis, not the Kural's.

kurals.tamil:
அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதேதம் மக்கள்
சிறுகை அளாவிய கூழ்.
kurals.transliteration:
Amizhdhinum Aatra Inidhedham Makkal,
Sirukai Alaaviya Koozh.
kurals.meaning: Far sweeter than the nectar of the gods is plain boiled food that one's own children have stirred about with their little hands.
kurals.elementary: Imagine the most delicious dessert in the world — the kind a king would eat. Now imagine ordinary rice that your little brother or sister has squished and messed up with their tiny fingers. This kural says the messy rice tastes better. Not because of the rice — because of whose hands were in it.
kurals.university: This is perhaps the most quoted couplet in the Kural's domestic chapters, and its power lies in a calculated collision of registers. அமிழ்து (amiḻtu, Sanskrit amṛta) is the immortalising nectar of the gods, the top of the classical scale of sweetness; கூழ் (kūḻ) is at the bottom — a thin boiled gruel or mash, the plainest food in the Tamil larder. Between them Valluvar inserts the word that does all the work: அளாவிய (aḷāviya), "stirred, mixed about, dabbled in" by a சிறுகை, a "small hand." Parimēlaḻakar glosses அளாவல் by quoting a Puṟanāṉūṟu line about a child "dropping and touching and mouthing and churning" the ghee-rice until it is smeared everywhere — that is, he understands the verse to be describing genuine mess, not a decorous gesture. The theological move is quietly radical: the transcendent standard of sweetness is beaten not by a better food but by a relationship, and the sensory language of the next two couplets (touch, hearing) shows Valluvar building a deliberate small phenomenology of parenthood through the bodily senses.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa's Kṛṣṇa cycle dwells on the infant god raiding the butter pots, smearing curds over himself and the household, and being caught with his hands in the food — and on Yaśodā's helpless delight at exactly this, which becomes the devotional mode called vātsalya, love in the manner of a parent for a small child.
hinduism.explanation: An entire branch of Hindu devotion is built on the claim that God is most lovable in the form of a messy toddler with food on his hands.
hinduism.tie_back: Both traditions locate supreme sweetness not in the food but in the small hands that have been in it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested narrative cycle rather than a quoted verse; the imagistic match — child, hands, food, parental delight — is remarkably close.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?”
christianity.explanation: Andrew points out a boy's plain, inadequate packed lunch — barley was the cheap grain — and that humble food from a child's hands becomes the meal that feeds five thousand.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts take the poorest imaginable food, pass it through a child's hands, and find it has become more than the finest fare.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim and the child-plus-plain-food image is genuinely parallel, but the Gospel's point is miraculous provision, not parental affection.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Allah, shower blessings upon us in our city, and in our fruits, in our mudd and in our sa', blessings upon blessings,” — and he would then give that fruit to the youngest of the children present.
islam.explanation: When the season's first fruit was brought to the Prophet, he would pray over it and then hand the choicest first taste not to an elder or a guest but to the smallest child in the room.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats food as something whose value is completed by a child's hands rather than by its own quality.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 1373b, Book of Pilgrimage (narrated by Abū Hurayrah)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Sunnah.com; a warm and specific food-and-children parallel, though about honouring a child rather than the parent's own pleasure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service? That ye shall say, It is the sacrifice of the LORD's passover.”
judaism.explanation: The Passover meal is legislated from the outset around the child's question, so that the family's central ritual dinner is structured by and for the children at the table.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions make the presence of children the thing that transforms an ordinary family meal into the sweetest one there is.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, but the link is structural (a meal organised around children) rather than the Kural's specific image of food touched by small hands.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ashokāvadāna a small boy named Jaya, playing in the dirt, sees the Buddha passing on alms round and, having nothing else, drops a handful of dust into his begging bowl as if it were food; the Buddha accepts it, and predicts the child will be reborn as the great emperor Aśoka.
buddhism.explanation: The offering is literally worthless and literally dirty, yet it is received as the most consequential gift in the story because of the hands and heart it came from.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, what a child's small hand has put into the food is worth incomparably more than the food itself.
buddhism.source: Ashokāvadāna, the gift of dust (Divyāvadāna, ch. 26)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a narrative from a post-canonical Sanskrit avadāna; thematically apt on the value of a child's touch on food, but the framework is merit-making, not domestic delight.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “for by day rich-crowned Demeter would anoint him with ambrosia as if he were the offspring of a god and breathe sweetly upon him as she held him in her bosom”
greek_mythology.explanation: Disguised as a nurse in the house of Celeus, the grieving goddess Demeter secretly feeds the infant Demophoön the food of the immortals, trying to make a mortal child divine.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greek scene runs the Kural's image in reverse — there a goddess gives ambrosia to a child, while Valluvar says a child's hands make plain gruel beat ambrosia outright.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn 2 (To Demeter), 235–237 (trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, 1914)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the shared vocabulary of ambrosia, a child, and feeding is striking, though the Greek hymn's logic is the mirror image of the Kural's.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And so plain savours bring us a pleasure equal to a luxurious diet, when all the pain due to want is removed; and bread and water produce the highest pleasure, when one who needs them puts them to his lips.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus argues that the pleasure of eating peaks with simple food properly met, and that expensive fare adds nothing to the actual quality of the experience.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts dethrone luxury food, though Valluvar's plain gruel wins by affection where Epicurus's bread wins by the analysis of desire.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus (trans. Cyril Bailey, 1926)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Bailey; a real parallel on plain food outranking luxury, but Epicurus has no interest in children and reaches the conclusion by a quite different route.

kurals.tamil:
மக்கள்மெய் தீண்டல் உடற்கின்பம் மற்றுஅவர்
சொற்கேட்டல் இன்பம் செவிக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Makkalmey Theendal Udarkinbam Matravar,
Sorkettal Inbam Sevikku.
kurals.meaning: To touch the body of one's children is the body's delight; to hear them speak is the ear's delight.
kurals.elementary: Your body has different ways of being happy. Hugging someone you love makes your whole self feel warm — that's happiness for your skin. Listening to someone you love chatter away makes your ears happy. This kural says children give you both at once.
kurals.university: Valluvar constructs the couplet as a strict parallel built on two of the five senses: உடற்கு இன்பம் ("pleasure for the body") paired with செவிக்கு இன்பம் ("pleasure for the ear"), with தீண்டல் (tīṇṭal, touching) answering கேட்டல் (kēṭṭal, hearing). Read against kural 64, which handled taste, the three verses form a deliberate sensory triptych — the chapter argues for the value of children not by doctrine but by cataloguing the specific bodily goods they confer. Parimēlaḻakar makes an interesting interpretive choice here: he notes that Valluvar writes simply சொல் ("speech") rather than the மழலைச்சொல் ("lisping speech") of the following couplet, and concludes that the verse covers not only infant babble but the learned speech of grown children as well, so that the ear's pleasure lasts a lifetime. The grammatical abstract nouns தீண்டல் and கேட்டல் are, in his reading, standing by metonymy for the acts themselves — a small point of Tamil grammatical commentary that shows how closely this tradition read the couplets.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Kṛṣṇa childhood narratives Yaśodā's happiness is rendered almost entirely through the senses — the weight of the child on her hip, the smell of his hair, the sound of his prattle and of the anklet bells as he crawls — and these become the canonical images of vātsalya-bhāva, the devotional mood of parental love.
hinduism.explanation: Hindu devotional poetry treats the physical, sensory experience of handling and hearing a small child as a legitimate and even the highest form of religious feeling.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates the value of children in the concrete pleasures of touch and hearing rather than in abstract benefit.
hinduism.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8 and the vātsalya tradition
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a broad tradition rather than a single verse; the sensory emphasis genuinely matches, but it is devotional rather than the Kural's domestic register.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them.”
christianity.explanation: When the disciples try to keep children away from Jesus, he is indignant, and the Gospel records the physical detail — he picks them up and lays hands on them rather than merely speaking a blessing.
christianity.tie_back: Mark records the same instinct the Kural describes: with children, the body wants contact.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on the touching of children, though the ear-pleasure half of the couplet has no counterpart here.

islam.quote_or_event: Allah's Messenger kissed Al-Hasan bin 'Ali while Al-Aqra' bin Habis at-Tamim was sitting beside him. Al-Aqra said, “I have ten children and I have never kissed anyone of them.” Allah's Messenger cast a look at him and said, “Whoever is not merciful to others will not be treated mercifully.”
islam.explanation: A chief boasts of never having embraced any of his ten children, and is rebuked — physical tenderness toward children is treated here not as sentimentality but as a moral obligation.
islam.tie_back: The hadith defends precisely the bodily pleasure the Kural celebrates: the touch of one's children is a good, and refusing it is a fault.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 5997, Book of Good Manners (narrated by Abū Hurayrah)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Sunnah.com; an excellent match on touch, framed as mercy rather than as delight.

judaism.quote_or_event: “then shall ye suck, ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees. As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah reaches for the most immediate physical images available — nursing, being carried on the hip, being bounced on the knees — to describe the consolation God intends for Jerusalem.
judaism.tie_back: The prophet assumes exactly the Kural's premise: handling a small child is one of the most intensely good bodily experiences there is.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the tactile imagery matches closely, though it is deployed as a metaphor for divine comfort rather than as a claim about parenthood.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that every bond of affection — and the commentarial story attached to these verses concerns a man devastated by the death of his son — carries an exactly proportionate load of future sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the honest counter-voice to the Kural: the very sensory delight Valluvar praises is, for early Buddhism, the precise mechanism by which suffering gets in.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Included honestly as an inversion, not an echo — the renunciate strand of Buddhism directly contradicts this couplet, and there is no strong affirming parallel in the early canon.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Glorious Hector pulled the glittering helmet off and set it on the ground. Then he kissed his dear son and held him in his arms.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector reaches for his baby son on the walls of Troy; the child screams at the bronze and the nodding horsehair crest, so the greatest warrior of Troy takes off his helmet, laughing, in order to hold him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's line dramatised — a man who sets down his armour because the touch of his child is worth more.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 6.472–474 (trans. Ian Johnston, Vancouver Island University)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Johnston's published translation; one of the closest matches in the chapter for the couplet's tactile claim.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Thee now no more / The joyful house and best of wives shall welcome, / Nor little sons run up to snatch their kisses / And touch with silent happiness thy heart.”
philosophy.explanation: Lucretius is reporting — in order to refute — the standard human lament about death, and the thing he takes as the most obviously precious loss is small children running up to be kissed.
philosophy.tie_back: The Epicurean poet picks out the identical two goods the Kural does: the child's rush into your arms and the wordless delight it produces.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 3.894–896 (trans. William Ellery Leonard, 1916)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against the Leonard translation; an unusually precise philosophical parallel, with the caveat that Lucretius cites it in order to argue it should not be feared to lose.

kurals.tamil:
குழல்இனிது யாழ்இனிது என்பதம் மக்கள்
மழலைச்சொல் கேளா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kuzhalinidhu Yaazhinidhu Enpadham Makkal,
Mazhalaichchol Kelaadhavar.
kurals.meaning: "The flute is sweet, the lute is sweet" — so say only those who have never heard the lisping speech of their own children.
kurals.elementary: Some people say the most beautiful sound in the world is music. This kural teases them a little: they only think that because they have never sat and listened to a toddler talking nonsense. If they had, they would know which sound really wins.
kurals.university: The couplet is the Kural's most famous piece of wit, and its structure is a rhetorical trap. Valluvar never asserts that a child's babble is sweeter than music; he simply reports who it is that ranks music first — namely, those who have not heard மழலைச்சொல் (maḻalai-c-col), the half-formed lisping speech of a small child. Parimēlaḻakar identifies the remainder as a குறிப்பெச்சம், a deliberately unspoken implication that the reader is left to supply, and Maṇakkuṭavar makes it blunt: "those who have heard do not say it." The two instruments named are not decorative: the குழல் (kuḻal, the transverse flute) and the யாழ் (yāḻ, the ancient Tamil harp-lute) were the paired standards of vocal-and-instrumental excellence in the Caṅkam musical system, so Valluvar is measuring the child's voice against the recognised summit of the art. The word maḻalai has since passed into ordinary Tamil as an affectionate term for toddler-speech largely on the strength of this verse.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kṛṣṇa's flute is treated across Vaiṣṇava poetry as the most irresistible sound in creation, drawing cows, rivers and gopīs out of themselves; yet in the same literature Yaśodā's happiness comes not from the flute at all but from her child's broken half-words and the noise of his anklets.
hinduism.explanation: The devotional tradition holds both claims at once — the flute as supreme music, and the child's voice as what a mother actually treasures.
hinduism.tie_back: The two sounds the Kural sets against each other, flute and toddler-speech, are the same two that Hindu devotion places side by side in the Kṛṣṇa cycle.
hinduism.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8–10.21 (the flute of Kṛṣṇa and Yaśodā's vātsalya)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A genuine and pleasing image-level resonance, but the tradition never stages the comparison as a contest the way Valluvar does; scored low for that reason.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Yea; have ye never read, Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise?”
christianity.explanation: The chief priests are indignant at children shouting in the temple; Jesus answers by citing scripture to the effect that infant voices are the medium through which praise reaches its completed form.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts rank the untrained sound of small children above the accomplished performances of adults.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a real match on the surpassing value of children's voices, though framed as worship rather than as domestic sweetness.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Jesus] said, 'Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.'”
islam.explanation: Mary, challenged over her newborn, points to the infant; and the child in the cradle speaks — the Qur'an's most striking instance of a baby's voice silencing a crowd of adults.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's premise that an infant's speech carries a weight no adult performance can match, though for the Qur'an the weight is miraculous rather than affectionate.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, but this is an articulate miracle, essentially the opposite of the endearing unintelligibility that the Tamil word maḻalai denotes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength because of thine enemies, that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm places the voices of the very youngest at the centre of a poem about cosmic majesty, making infant sound a source of strength rather than mere noise.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it deliberately elevates the least trained human voice above everything more impressive.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the elevation of infant speech matches, but the psalm's frame is theological power, not the ear's pleasure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Buddha returned to Kapilavatthu, Yasodharā sent their young son Rāhula to him saying that he should ask his father for his inheritance; the boy followed the Buddha through the city repeating the request, and the Buddha's answer was to have him ordained, giving him the Dhamma instead.
buddhism.explanation: The scene is one of very few in the early canon that lingers on a small child's persistent, artless speech to a parent.
buddhism.tie_back: It offers the Kural's situation — a father hearing his small son's voice — but the tradition treats the moment as an occasion for renunciation rather than for delight.
buddhism.source: Vinaya, Mahāvagga I.54 (the ordination of Rāhula)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Deliberately scored low and honestly: the early Buddhist canon has no praise of a child's babble, and this is the closest scene available rather than a true parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The satyr Marsyas, having taken up the aulos (the reed pipe), challenged Apollo and his lyre to decide which instrument was sweeter; Apollo won and flayed him alive for the presumption.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth stages the question of pipe versus lyre as a literal contest, and treats the answer as so serious that the loser is destroyed for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar names the same two categories of instrument, pipe and stringed lute, and then dismisses the whole contest — neither wins against a toddler talking.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the myth; the pipe-versus-lute framing is an unusually exact coincidence with the Kural's two instruments, but children play no part in the Greek story.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius, describing how early humans first softened, writes that it was the coming of children and the winning ways of their affection that broke down the fierce, proud temper of primitive men and made settled life possible.
philosophy.explanation: For the Epicurean poet, the charm of small children is a causal force in human history, not a sentimental aside — it is what taught the species gentleness.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives a naturalistic account of why the Kural's claim is true: children's artless voices and gestures really do disarm adults in a way art cannot.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased because translations of this passage diverge; the argument is faithfully represented but concerns social history rather than the comparison with music.

kurals.tamil:
தந்தை மகற்காற்றும் நன்றி அவையத்து
முந்தி இருப்பச் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thandhai Makarkaatrum Nandri Avaiyaththu,
Mundhi Iruppach Cheyal.
kurals.meaning: The good that a father owes his son is to make him fit to sit in the front rank of the assembly of the learned.
kurals.elementary: A dad can give his child lots of things — toys, money, a bike. This kural says the best gift is different: teach your child so well that when clever grown-ups sit down to talk, your child is the one they want sitting at the front.
kurals.university: The couplet defines the father's duty with unusual precision. நன்றி (naṉṟi) here means the benefit or good office a father performs, and the content of that benefit is not property but standing: to be able to sit முந்தி (muntī, "foremost, ahead") in the அவை (avai), the learned assembly. The avai was a real institution in the Tamil and broader Indic world — the court or scholarly council where reputation was won by demonstrated learning and skill in speech — and the Kural devotes two later chapters, அவையறிதல் and அவையஞ்சாமை, to how one conducts oneself there. Parimēlaḻakar draws the sharpest possible conclusion from the wording: making a son wealthy, he says, cannot count as நன்றி at all, because wealth brings suffering; only education does. The couplet thus quietly converts the entire chapter's language of "wealth" into a claim about cultural capital, and it is this verse, with 68, that makes Chapter 7 one of the most-cited passages in modern Tamil arguments for universal education.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Uddālaka Āruṇi tells his son Śvetaketu, at twelve years old, to go and live as a student, on the grounds that in their family no one has ever remained unlearned — no one has been a brahmin merely by birth; the boy returns at twenty-four full of learning and conceited with it, whereupon his father begins the teaching that culminates in tat tvam asi.
hinduism.explanation: The father's obligation in this foundational Upaniṣadic scene is specifically educational: he will not permit his son to hold a status he has not earned by study.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural's rule enacted — the father's gift to the son is the learning that lets him stand among the learned in his own right.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Described rather than quoted because the standard translations of 6.1.1 differ noticeably; the scene is an exceptionally close match for the couplet's claim about a father's duty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.”
christianity.explanation: Paul addresses fathers directly and makes formation — instruction and discipline — the specific content of the paternal role, over against mere authority.
christianity.tie_back: Both verses single out the father and define his duty as the shaping of the child rather than the provision of goods.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on the father's formative duty, but the aim is religious upbringing rather than the Kural's public standing among scholars.

islam.quote_or_event: “No father has given a greater gift to his children than good moral training.”
islam.explanation: The hadith ranks the cultivation of a child's character above every material provision a father might make.
islam.tie_back: Both texts define the father's best gift as formation rather than inheritance.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Sunnah.com, but honestly flagged: this hadith is graded weak (ḍaʿīf) by adh-Dhahabī and al-Albānī, and its emphasis is manners rather than learning.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A father is obligated with regard to his son to circumcise him, and to redeem him if he is a firstborn son who must be redeemed by payment to a priest, and to teach him Torah, and to marry him to a woman, and to teach him a trade.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud lists the father's legal duties as a closed set, and two of the five are educational — Torah study and a marketable craft.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the father's obligation to his son concrete, enumerable, and centred on equipping him to hold his own place in the community.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against the Sefaria text; an excellent match on the framing of paternal duty as formation, though it includes ritual obligations the Kural has no interest in.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigālovāda Sutta the Buddha lists the five ways parents show compassion to their children: they restrain them from evil, encourage them to do good, have them trained in a profession, arrange a suitable marriage, and in due time hand over their inheritance.
buddhism.explanation: This is the fullest statement of lay parental duty in the Pali canon, and professional training sits at its centre.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts define what a parent owes a child as a duty of equipping them for a public role, not simply of loving or feeding them.
buddhism.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (the six directions: parents)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested list whose English wording varies by translator; a strong structural match, though 'a profession' is narrower than the Kural's assembly of the learned.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For this reason he sent me to instruct you in all these things, to be both a speaker of words and a doer of deeds.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The old tutor Phoenix reminds Achilles that Peleus sent him along precisely because the boy was untaught in war and in the assemblies where men win distinction — so Phoenix was to make him excellent at both speech and action.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Homeric father's stated aim for his son is the Kural's word for word: to hold the first place in the assembly.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 9.442–443 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1924)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against the Murray Loeb rendering; the reference to assemblies 'where men become preeminent' in the preceding lines makes this the chapter's closest Greek parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “As soon as one of them grasps what is said to him, the nurse, the mother, the tutor, and the father himself strive hard that the child may excel, and as each act and word occurs they teach and impress upon him that this is just, and that unjust, one thing noble, another base, one holy, another unholy, and that he is to do this, and not do that.”
philosophy.explanation: Protagoras is arguing that virtue is taught, and his evidence is the sheer relentlessness with which Athenian households instruct their children from the first moment they can understand language.
philosophy.tie_back: It supplies the argumentative backing for the Kural's assumption that a child's eventual standing among the learned is something a father actively makes.
philosophy.source: Plato, Protagoras 325c–d (trans. W. R. M. Lamb, Loeb Classical Library)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against the Perseus text; matches on the father's duty to form the child, though Protagoras is describing practice in order to win a debate about whether virtue is teachable.

kurals.tamil:
தம்மின்தம் மக்கள் அறிவுடைமை மாநிலத்து
மன்னுயிர்க் கெல்லாம் இனிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Thammindham Makkal Arivudaimai Maanilaththu,
Mannuyirk Kellaam Inidhu.
kurals.meaning: That one's children should be wiser than oneself is sweet not only to the parents but to every living being on this great earth.
kurals.elementary: When you get better at something than your teacher or your parents, nobody minds — everyone is delighted. This kural says that is one of the few kinds of being-beaten that makes the whole world happy.
kurals.university: The compressed opening தம்மின்தம் மக்கள் அறிவுடைமை carries an ambiguity the commentators split over. Parimēlaḻakar reads தம்மின் as "more than to themselves" — the children's wisdom is sweeter to all the world's beings than it is even to the parents — and takes மன்னுயிர் ("enduring lives") to stand specifically for the discerning, since only they can appreciate learning. Most moderns, including M. Varadarajan and Karunanidhi, read தம்மின் comparatively of the children instead: that the children surpass the parents in wisdom. Either way, the verse performs a striking widening of scope. Having spent four couplets on the private senses — taste, touch, hearing — Valluvar suddenly extends the circle to மாநிலத்து மன்னுயிர்க்கெல்லாம், every living thing on the great earth. The claim is that a child's intelligence is a non-rival public good: unlike wealth or rank, one family's gain in wisdom costs no one anything and delights everyone. That move, from the household to the biosphere in a single line, is characteristic of the Kural's method throughout the household chapters.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The boy Naciketas, sent in anger to Death by his father Vājaśravasa after questioning the worthlessness of the cows his father was giving away, refuses Yama's offers of wealth, long life and pleasure, and holds out for the knowledge of what lies beyond death — obtaining a teaching that surpasses anything his father possessed.
hinduism.explanation: The Upaniṣad's entire teaching is delivered to a child precisely because the child's discernment outstrips the adult world around him.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the text takes evident pleasure in a son whose wisdom exceeds his father's.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the framing narrative; the son-surpasses-father theme is unmistakable, though the Upaniṣad presents it through conflict rather than universal delight.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions. And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.”
christianity.explanation: The only episode the Gospels record from Jesus' childhood is this one: a twelve-year-old sitting among the teachers in the temple, and the reaction is astonishment from everyone present, not just his parents.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's scenario almost exactly — a child's understanding delighting an entire assembly beyond the family.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the widening of delight from parents to all who heard him matches the couplet's second line closely.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Allah] said, 'O John, take the Scripture with determination.' And We gave him judgement [while yet] a boy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents Yaḥyā (John) as receiving ḥukm — sound judgement and discernment — while still a child, an explicit divine endorsement of precocious wisdom.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat a child's wisdom outrunning ordinary adult expectation as something good, given, and worth announcing.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on a child's exceptional wisdom, though the Qur'an does not draw the comparison to the parents that the Kural makes central.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the child Samuel grew on, and was in favour both with the LORD, and also with men.”
judaism.explanation: Samuel, given over to the sanctuary as a small child, grows into the prophetic authority that his elders — including the priest Eli and Eli's own sons — conspicuously lack.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a child's growing discernment is recorded as a good that reaches beyond his family to everyone around him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a real match on a child's wisdom gladdening the wider community, but the parental comparison is implicit rather than stated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The Wise desire a child that is / Superior or just the same, / But not for one inferior, / Who will break up the family”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha classifies children into three kinds — atijāta (born beyond, surpassing the parents), anujāta (born after, equal to them), and avajāta (born below) — and says the wise hope for the first.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact thesis, in a canonical taxonomy: the child who exceeds the parent is the one to be wished for.
buddhism.source: Itivuttaka 74, Puttasutta, vv. 504–505 (trans. Ānandajoti Bhikkhu, Buddhist Wisdom Verses)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the Pali category atijāta — the child born superior to the parents — is as close a technical parallel to this couplet as the cross-tradition search produced.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the day he is born, the infant Hermes climbs out of his cradle, invents the lyre from a tortoise shell, steals Apollo's cattle and covers his tracks by making them walk backwards, then argues his own case before Zeus so cleverly that Zeus laughs aloud with delight and the gods settle the quarrel in friendship.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Homeric Hymn is essentially a comedy about a newborn whose intelligence outmatches an established Olympian's, and whose father's reaction is open delight.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the child's surpassing wit is pleasing to everyone who witnesses it, not only to the parent.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the hymn's narrative; the delight of a father in a child who outsmarts his elders matches well, though the Greek child's cleverness is thievish rather than learned.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates takes an untaught slave boy from Meno's household, asks him a series of questions about doubling the area of a square, and draws a correct geometrical demonstration out of him — to the visible astonishment of Meno, who had assumed the boy knew nothing.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the scene to argue that understanding is latent in every person, so that a child of no standing can be shown to possess what the educated master does not expect.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts stage the pleasure and surprise of finding wisdom in someone from whom no one expected it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Accurate paraphrase, but the boy is not Meno's child and Plato's interest is the theory of recollection, so the parental dimension of the couplet is absent.

kurals.tamil:
ஈன்ற பொழுதின் பெரிதுவக்கும் தன்மகனைச்
சான்றோன் எனக்கேட்ட தாய்.
kurals.transliteration:
Eendra Pozhudhin Peridhuvakkum Thanmakanaich,
Chaandron Enakketta Thaai.
kurals.meaning: A mother who hears her son spoken of as a person of true worth rejoices more in that moment than she did in the hour she gave birth to him.
kurals.elementary: The day a baby is born is one of the happiest days a mother ever has. But this kural says there is a day that beats it: the day she overhears other people saying her child has grown up to be a genuinely good person.
kurals.university: The couplet's force comes from the word சான்றோன் (cāṉṟōṉ), from the root சால் — "filled up, complete, sufficient." A cāṉṟōṉ is not merely a clever or successful man but one who is full in character, and the term carries enormous weight in Tamil ethical vocabulary; the Kural devotes a whole later chapter, சான்றாண்மை, to the quality. The second load-bearing word is கேட்ட (kēṭṭa, "having heard"): the mother's supreme joy arrives not from seeing but from hearing others say it. Parimēlaḻakar reads this carefully, arguing that the ordinary joy of birth is the joy of what is seen with the eyes on one's lap, while this is the distinct and greater joy of hearing one's child pronounced complete by those qualified to judge. He also notes that the couplet names the mother specifically because her joy admits of no measure, which is why Valluvar separates it from the father's case in 67. Read alongside 70, the chapter closes with a matched pair — the mother's joy, then the father's requital — with public reputation as the currency of both.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kausalyā's happiness in the Rāmāyaṇa is repeatedly portrayed not as pride in having borne a prince but as joy at the universal testimony of Ayodhyā's people to Rāma's righteousness — and her deepest grief, at his exile, is grief at being separated from a son whom everyone calls good.
hinduism.explanation: The epic consistently locates a mother's happiness in what the community says about her son's character rather than in his rank or her own act of bearing him.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make the mother's great joy depend on hearing her son publicly reckoned a man of worth.
hinduism.source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa (Kausalyā and Rāma)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a theme running through the epic rather than a single citable verse; thematically apt but diffuse, hence the modest score.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.”
christianity.explanation: The elder writing to Gaius reports that travelling brethren have brought back news of Gaius's conduct, and says that receiving such a report is the height of his happiness.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact structure — the joy is in hearing the report of a child's moral worth, and it is named as the greatest joy there is.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on both the mechanism (hearing a report) and the superlative claim, differing only in that the speaker is a spiritual father.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when she delivered her, she said, 'My Lord, I have delivered a female.' And Allah was most knowing of what she delivered... Every time Zechariah entered upon her in the prayer chamber, he found with her provision. He said, 'O Mary, from where is this [coming] to you?'”
islam.explanation: The wife of ʿImrān dedicates her child before birth and is initially disappointed at the outcome; the narrative then vindicates the daughter through Zechariah's repeated astonishment at Mary's standing with God.
islam.tie_back: It touches the Kural's theme — a mother's estimate of her child transformed by what is later witnessed of that child's worth — but only obliquely.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim but honestly weak: it is Zechariah, not the mother, who marvels, and the joy-at-hearing-praise structure of the Kural is not present.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The father of the righteous shall greatly rejoice: and he that begetteth a wise child shall have joy of him. Thy father and thy mother shall be glad, and she that bare thee shall rejoice.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb moves from the general case to a direct address, and singles out the woman who gave birth as the one who will rejoice.
judaism.tie_back: The phrase "she that bare thee shall rejoice" is almost a translation of the Kural's ஈன்ற... தாய் — the one who bore you, rejoicing at your wisdom.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; an exceptionally close verbal and conceptual match, lacking only the Kural's explicit comparison with the hour of birth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Rūpasārī, the brahmin mother of Sāriputta, had long resented her son's renunciation; on the night of his death in the room where he was born, she saw the great deities of the heavens come in succession to attend him, realised what her son actually was, and only then rejoiced in him — after which he taught her and she attained stream-entry.
buddhism.explanation: The commentarial tradition preserves this as the story of a mother who came late and overwhelmingly to the knowledge of her son's true stature.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the mother's supreme joy arrive not at birth but at the moment her son is recognised for what he has become.
buddhism.source: Pali commentarial tradition on Sāriputta's death (Dhammapada Commentary; see also SN 47.13)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a post-canonical commentarial narrative rather than a canonical text, and the recognition comes by vision rather than by report; scored accordingly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “She then, seized with wonder, went back to her chamber, for she laid to heart the wise saying of her son.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope has come down to ask the bard to stop his song; Telemachus, for the first time in the poem, answers her as a grown man and sends her back upstairs — and Homer records that what she takes away is not offence but amazement at his wisdom.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's moment precisely: a mother's wonder at hearing her son reveal himself as a man of sense.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 1.360 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1919)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against the Murray Loeb text; she hears him directly rather than hearing others praise him, which is the one gap.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that mothers who have given their children away to be raised elsewhere go on loving them and rejoice when they recognise them prospering, without ever seeking to be loved in return — because loving, rather than being loved, is what the affection of a parent consists in.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle a mother's characteristic pleasure is in the child's good as such, not in any benefit she receives from it.
philosophy.tie_back: It explains philosophically why the Kural's mother rejoices at a report she gains nothing from — it is the good of the child, heard about, that constitutes the joy.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased since translations of the passage differ; the analysis of maternal love matches well, but Aristotle is not comparing that joy with the joy of childbirth.

kurals.tamil:
மகன்தந்தைக்கு ஆற்றும் உதவி இவன்தந்தை
என்நோற்றான் கொல்எனும் சொல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Makandhandhaikku Aatrum Udhavi Ivandhandhai,
Ennotraan Kol Enum Sol.
kurals.meaning: The service a son renders his father is to live so that people say, "What austerities must this man's father have performed, to deserve such a son?"
kurals.elementary: How does a child pay a parent back? Not with money. This kural says you pay them back by being so good that when people meet you they think, "Wow — whoever raised this person must have done something really special."
kurals.university: The chapter closes by completing the reciprocal pair begun in 67: there the father's duty was to place the son foremost in the assembly; here the son's உதவி (utavi, "help, requital") is to generate a particular sentence in other people's mouths. The verb நோல் / நோற்றல் (nōṟṟal) means to undertake tapas — ascetic austerity, penance — so என்நோற்றான் கொல் literally asks "what penance can he have performed?" The idiom presumes the karmic economy in which a son of high quality is earned by merit, and Valluvar's wit is to make the son's whole filial duty consist in causing that inference to be drawn. Parimēlaḻakar underlines the point that the requital is owed specifically to the father who made him learned — i.e. it answers couplet 67 directly — and he glosses சொல் as standing, by metonymy, for the conduct that produces the saying. Note what the couplet conspicuously does not say: nothing about supporting parents in old age, obedience, or ritual duty. The entire obligation is discharged through character as publicly perceived, which is a strikingly reputational, non-transactional construal of filial piety.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Daśaratha, childless and aging, performs the putrakāmeṣṭi sacrifice under Ṛṣyaśṛṅga to obtain sons, and receives Rāma and his brothers; thereafter the people of Ayodhyā speak of Rāma's virtues in terms that reflect glory back onto the father who obtained him by austerity.
hinduism.explanation: The epic supplies the literal background the Kural's idiom assumes — a father who performed rites and austerities in order to deserve a son, and a son whose excellence publicly vindicates them.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's imagined bystander asking what penance the father performed is asking exactly the question Daśaratha's story answers.
hinduism.source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla Kāṇḍa (the putrakāmeṣṭi of Daśaratha)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode rather than a quoted verse; the tapas-for-a-son framework it supplies is precisely the one the couplet's idiom presupposes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
christianity.explanation: At the Jordan, the father's satisfaction in the son is declared publicly, before the crowd, at the moment the son begins his work.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts make the son's worth into a public utterance that redounds to the father, though here the father speaks rather than the onlookers.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the direction is reversed — the father praises the son rather than bystanders inferring the father's merit from the son.

islam.quote_or_event: “And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, 'My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up [when I was] small.'”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an prescribes the son's requital to his parents in old age as humility and intercessory prayer, framed as repayment for the upbringing he received.
islam.tie_back: Both texts define what a grown child owes a parent, though the Qur'an makes it prayer and deference while the Kural makes it reputation.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a solid match on the son's duty of requital, but its content is quite different from the Kural's purely reputational answer.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb states the return on parenting in the simplest possible form: the child's character is what the parent receives.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts make the son's standing, rather than any material support, the thing the parent actually gets back.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; close on the principle of requital through character, though it lacks the Kural's distinctive public-saying mechanism.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says that even if one carried one's mother on one shoulder and one's father on the other for a hundred years, tending them the whole time, one would still not have repaid them; but whoever establishes parents who lack faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom in those four things has repaid them and more.
buddhism.explanation: Physical service is declared structurally insufficient as repayment; only raising the parents' own moral and spiritual condition counts.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it rejects material or bodily support as the true filial return and substitutes something the son achieves in the realm of character.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.34 (Book of the Twos, on repaying one's parents)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested discourse whose English wordings vary; a strong conceptual match, differing in that the Buddha's repayment acts directly on the parents rather than through public reputation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Zeus, all you other gods, grant that this child, my son, may become, like me, pre-eminent among the Trojans, as strong and brave as me. Grant that he may rule Troy with strength. May people someday say, as he returns from war, 'This man is far better than his father.'”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector, holding his infant son on the walls of Troy, prays not that the boy honour him but that strangers one day judge the son superior to the father — and counts that as the outcome he most wants.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's mechanism exactly: the son discharges his debt by causing a particular sentence to be said about him in public, which redounds to the father.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 6.476–481 (trans. Ian Johnston, Vancouver Island University)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Johnston's published translation; the closest parallel in the chapter — both verses make the father's reward a saying uttered by onlookers about the son.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Would anyone have heard of Aristo and Gryllus except through Xenophon and Plato, their sons? Socrates keeps alive the memory of Sophroniscus.”
philosophy.explanation: Arguing that a son can repay and even surpass what his father gave him, Seneca points out that many fathers are remembered only because of what their sons became, citing Agrippa’s obscure father alongside the fathers of Plato, Xenophon and Socrates.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s idea of a son’s service exactly: the child’s worth becomes the way the world comes to honour the parent.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits (De Beneficiis), Book III, ch. 32 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (On Benefits/Book III, Stewart). Seneca frames this as a son's benefit to his father that brings the father lasting fame, which is a close match to the Kural; the specific 'what penance did his father do' exclamation is not in Seneca.
